title: Estimate decimal sums and differences by rounding or benchmarks

lesson.title: Guess Smart: Estimating with Decimals

steps.say: You already know how to compare and order decimals to thousandths, so you can tell which whole number a decimal is sitting closest to. Today we use that skill to guess a total quickly, without doing the whole careful adding.

Here is the one move. Put your decimal on a number line and see which end it is closer to. Four point eight five is squished way over near five, so we say it is about five. That closest whole number is our friendly stand in.

visual.caption: 4.85 is much closer to 5 than to 4

steps.say: Let us go shopping. A carton of milk costs four dollars and eighty-five cents, and a loaf of bread costs three dollars and ten cents. Milk slides to five dollars, bread slides to three dollars, and five plus three is eight. So about eight dollars. That took two seconds!

visual.caption: Start at the 5 dollars, hop 3 more, land near 8

steps.say: Now the thinking part. Was our guess a little high or a little low? We pushed four point eight five up by fifteen cents, and we pulled three point ten down by only ten cents. We pushed up more than we pulled down, so eight dollars is a tiny bit too much. The real total is seven ninety-five, just under eight. Our reasoning was right!

visual.caption: The true total, 7.95, sits just under our estimate of 8

steps.say: Here is a mistake I see a lot. Some kids just chop the decimal off. They see two point eight seven five minus one point zero four and say two minus one equals one. But look at the number line, two point eight seven five is almost at three, not at two! Round it properly and you get three minus one, which is two. The true answer is one point eight three five, so two is a great guess and one is way off.

visual.caption: Do not chop to 2 — 2.875 rounds up to 3

steps.say: So remember, slide each decimal to its closest whole number, then add or subtract the easy way.

lesson.answer: Slide each decimal to its nearest whole number on the number line, then add or subtract — fast, and close enough to check your answer.

practice.question: On Saturday you walk three point eight six kilometres to the beach, then two point one five kilometres home along the seawall. Draw a number line from three to four and mark three point eight six, then draw one from two to three and mark two point one five. Which whole number is each one closest to? Use them to estimate the total distance you walked.
practice.answer: Three point eight six is closest to four, and two point one five is closest to two. Four plus two is six, so you walked about six kilometres. (The exact total is six point zero one kilometres — our estimate was almost perfect, because rounding one number up by about the same amount we rounded the other down cancels out.)
